title: K-Nearest Neighbours

blocks.t: From the notes
KNN, as written
KNN — K Nearest Neighbours.

It is a lazy learner — it does not learn anything in the
training phase, it just stores the data. All the work happens at
prediction time.
To predict a new point:

items:
Calculate the distance from the new point to every
training point.

Classification $\to$ majority vote.
Regression $\to$ mean of their values.

blocks.t: Feature scaling is compulsory — distance depends on units.

The whole method rests on one assumption: points that are close together
have similar labels. Nothing more. There is no model, no coefficients, no loss
function — the training data is the model.

That makes KNN a non-parametric method: the number of things it
remembers grows with the data instead of being fixed in advance. And it makes it
a lazy learner: fit() is just a copy, while predict()
does all the work. Every other algorithm in this course is the opposite —
expensive to train, cheap to predict.
Distance metrics

For two points $x,z \in \mathbb{R}^d$ the Minkowski distance of order
$p$ is
d_p(x,z)=\left(\sum_{j=1}^{d} |x_j - z_j|^{p}\right)^{1/p}.

items:
$p=1$: Manhattan (city block) — $\sum_j |x_j-z_j|$. More robust
to outliers in a single dimension, and often better in high dimensions.

blocks.t:
For binary/categorical data use Hamming distance (number of differing
attributes); for text or any setting where magnitude is irrelevant use
cosine distance $1-\frac{x\cdot z}{\|x\|\|z\|}$.

Minkowski with $p<1$ is not a metric — it violates the triangle inequality —
but fractional distances are sometimes used deliberately in very high dimensions
because they preserve contrast better than Euclidean. This is a research
curiosity, not a default.
The role of k

blocks.cap:
The same data, five values of k. At $k=1$ every training point owns a
cell of a Voronoi diagram and training error is exactly zero. At $k=n$ every
prediction is the global majority class.

blocks.t: k is the bias–variance dial

Small k $\to$ flexible boundary, low bias, high
variance. $k=1$ fits noise perfectly: move one training point and the boundary
moves with it.

Large k $\to$ smooth boundary, high bias, low
variance. $k=n$ ignores the input entirely and predicts the majority class.

Effective model complexity is roughly $n/k$, so $k$ behaves like an
inverse complexity parameter — the opposite direction to
max_depth or the degree of a polynomial. Choose it by cross-validation,
never by training error, which always picks $k=1$.

Ties. With two classes an even $k$ can tie. Use an odd $k$ for binary
classification. With more than two classes odd $k$ does not guarantee anything;
sklearn breaks ties by picking the smallest class label, which is arbitrary —
weights="distance" makes ties essentially impossible and is the cleaner
fix.
Scaling: not optional

blocks.cap:
Left: train/test/CV accuracy against k — training accuracy is a
useless guide. Middle: identical data and model, one feature multiplied by 250.
Right: uniform versus distance weighting in KNN regression.

blocks.t:
Why scaling matters more here than anywhere else. Suppose one feature
is salary in rupees ($10^5$ scale) and another is years of experience ($10^1$).
Squared Euclidean distance is
(\Delta\text{salary})^2 + (\Delta\text{experience})^2

and the first term is roughly $10^8$ times larger. Experience is arithmetically
present but has no influence whatsoever on which neighbours are chosen.
The model silently becomes 1-D. A linear model would just learn a small
coefficient and be fine; KNN has no coefficients to compensate with.

Use StandardScaler by default, MinMaxScaler when features are
bounded, RobustScaler when outliers are present — and always inside a
Pipeline, so the scaler is fitted on training folds only.
Weighted KNN

Uniform voting treats the 1st and the $k$th neighbour identically. Distance
weighting gives neighbour $i$ a weight $w_i = 1/d_i$ (or a kernel such as
$e^{-d_i^2/2h^2}$), and predicts

\hat y = \frac{\sum_{i\in N_k} w_i y_i}{\sum_{i\in N_k} w_i}
\quad\text{(regression)},
\qquad
\hat c = \arg\max_{c} \sum_{i \in N_k} w_i \mathbf{1}[y_i=c]
\quad\text{(classification)}.

This makes the prediction a continuous function of $x$ instead of a step
function, which is why the red curve in the right-hand panel above is smooth
where the blue one is a staircase. It also makes large $k$ much safer: distant
neighbours are included but barely counted.
The curse of dimensionality

blocks.cap:
Left: as dimension grows, the gap between the nearest and farthest
neighbour shrinks relative to the distance itself — "nearest" stops meaning
anything. Middle: measured accuracy with only 2 informative features and the
rest noise. Right: prediction cost, and why exact brute force does not scale.

blocks.t: For many distributions, as $d\to\infty$,
\frac{\mathbb{E}[d_{\max}] - \mathbb{E}[d_{\min}]}{\mathbb{E}[d_{\min}]} \longrightarrow 0 .

Every point becomes approximately equidistant from every other point, so the
$k$ "nearest" neighbours are barely nearer than random points.

A second way to see it: to keep a fixed fraction $r$ of the data inside a
neighbourhood in $d$ dimensions, the side length of the cube must be
$r^{1/d}$. To capture 1% of the data in 10 dimensions you need a cube covering
$0.01^{1/10}\approx 63\%$ of the range of every feature. That is not a
local neighbourhood in any meaningful sense.

KNN degrades from irrelevant features, not just from many features. Every
noise dimension adds variance to the distance and dilutes the informative ones.
Do aggressive feature selection, or reduce with PCA, before using KNN in more
than roughly 10–20 dimensions. Tree ensembles ignore irrelevant features almost
for free; KNN cannot.
Making prediction fast

head: Algorithm
Query cost
When to use
rows: Small $n$, very large $d$, or sparse data. Exact.
Low dimension ($d \lesssim 20$), Minkowski metrics only. Exact.
Higher dimension than KD, arbitrary metrics. Exact.
sklearn picks based on $n$, $d$ and the metric.
Millions of rows, approximate answers acceptable. Outside sklearn.

blocks.t:
A KD-tree splits space by axis-aligned hyperplanes, alternating
dimensions. To answer a query it descends to the leaf containing the point, then
backtracks — but only into branches whose bounding box could contain something
closer than the best found so far. In low dimensions that prunes almost
everything. In high dimensions the hypersphere around the query intersects
nearly every box, nothing is pruned, and the tree becomes slower than brute
force because of the overhead. A Ball tree uses nested hyperspheres
instead of boxes, which prune better in higher dimensions and work with any
metric.
Code

import numpy as np
from sklearn.datasets import make_moons, load_wine
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split, GridSearchCV, cross_val_score
from sklearn.neighbors import (KNeighborsClassifier, KNeighborsRegressor,
                               NearestNeighbors, RadiusNeighborsClassifier)
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.metrics import classification_report

# ==================================================================
# 1. KNN FROM SCRATCH -- the algorithm is 10 lines
# ==================================================================
class MyKNN:
    def __init__(self, k=5, p=2, weights="uniform"):
        self.k, self.p, self.weights = k, p, weights

    def fit(self, X, y):
        self.X, self.y = np.asarray(X, float), np.asarray(y)   # "just store it"
        self.classes_ = np.unique(self.y)
        return self

    def _dist(self, q):
        # Minkowski distance from q to every stored point
        return (np.abs(self.X - q) ** self.p).sum(axis=1) ** (1 / self.p)

    def predict(self, Q):
        out = []
        for q in np.asarray(Q, float):
            d   = self._dist(q)
            idx = np.argpartition(d, self.k)[:self.k]     # O(n), not a full sort
            w   = np.ones(self.k) if self.weights == "uniform" else 1.0 / (d[idx] + 1e-12)
            # weighted majority vote
            scores = {c: w[self.y[idx] == c].sum() for c in self.classes_}
            out.append(max(scores, key=scores.get))
        return np.array(out)

X, y = make_moons(400, noise=0.28, random_state=0)
Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.3, random_state=0)
print("scratch:", (MyKNN(5).fit(Xtr, ytr).predict(Xte) == yte).mean())
print("sklearn:",  KNeighborsClassifier(5).fit(Xtr, ytr).score(Xte, yte))

# ==================================================================
# 2. THE CORRECT PIPELINE -- scaler INSIDE, so it never sees the val fold
# ==================================================================
pipe = Pipeline([("sc",  StandardScaler()),
                 ("knn", KNeighborsClassifier())])

grid = {
    "knn__n_neighbors": list(range(1, 41, 2)),   # odd values for binary
    "knn__weights":     ["uniform", "distance"],
    "knn__p":           [1, 2],                  # Manhattan / Euclidean
    "knn__metric":      ["minkowski"],
}
wine = load_wine()
gs = GridSearchCV(pipe, grid, cv=5, scoring="accuracy", n_jobs=4)
gs.fit(wine.data, wine.target)
print("best params:", gs.best_params_)
print("best CV    :", round(gs.best_score_, 4))

# What scaling was worth, measured:
raw = cross_val_score(KNeighborsClassifier(**{k.split("__")[1]: v
        for k, v in gs.best_params_.items()}), wine.data, wine.target, cv=5).mean()
print("unscaled CV:", round(raw, 4), " scaled CV:", round(gs.best_score_, 4))

# ==================================================================
# 3. REGRESSION
# ==================================================================
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
Xr = np.sort(rng.uniform(0, 10, 200))[:, None]
yr = np.sin(Xr.ravel()) + rng.normal(0, 0.2, 200)
for w in ("uniform", "distance"):
    r = KNeighborsRegressor(n_neighbors=9, weights=w).fit(Xr[:150], yr[:150])
    print(w, "R2:", round(r.score(Xr[150:], yr[150:]), 4))

# ==================================================================
# 4. RADIUS NEIGHBOURS -- fixed radius instead of fixed k
# ==================================================================
# Better when density varies a lot: dense regions vote with many neighbours,
# sparse regions with few. Points with an EMPTY radius need outlier_label.
rn = RadiusNeighborsClassifier(radius=1.0, weights="distance",
                               outlier_label="most_frequent").fit(Xtr, ytr)
print("radius-KNN:", round(rn.score(Xte, yte), 4))

# ==================================================================
# 5. USING THE NEIGHBOUR STRUCTURE DIRECTLY
# ==================================================================
nn = NearestNeighbors(n_neighbors=6, algorithm="ball_tree").fit(Xtr)
dist, idx = nn.kneighbors(Xte[:3])
print("distances to 6 nearest:", dist.round(3))

# The k-distance plot -- used to pick eps for DBSCAN (Topic 78) and to
# spot outliers: points whose k-th neighbour is unusually far away.
d_k = np.sort(nn.kneighbors(Xtr)[0][:, -1])
print("90th percentile k-distance:", round(np.percentile(d_k, 90), 3))

# ==================================================================
# 6. SCALING TO LARGE n  -- exact vs approximate
# ==================================================================
big = rng.normal(size=(100000, 12))
lab = (big[:, 0] + big[:, 1] > 0).astype(int)
exact = KNeighborsClassifier(10, algorithm="ball_tree", n_jobs=4).fit(big, lab)
# For millions of rows, exact search stops being viable. Use an approximate
# nearest-neighbour library instead -- faiss, hnswlib, annoy, scann -- which
# trade a small recall loss for orders-of-magnitude speed.
Everything on one page
Summary

Algorithm: store everything. To predict, compute the distance to all
$n$ training points, take the $k$ nearest, then majority-vote (classification)
or average (regression).

Lazy & non-parametric: $O(1)$ training, $O(nd)$ prediction. No
assumptions about the shape of the boundary — which is why it can fit any
shape given enough data, and why it needs a lot of data.

k is an inverse-complexity dial: $k{=}1$ overfits (zero training
error), $k{=}n$ underfits (majority class). Pick by cross-validation. Odd $k$
for binary problems, or use weights="distance".

Scaling is compulsory — distance is meaningless in mixed units, and
KNN has no coefficients to absorb the mismatch.

Dies in high dimensions. Distances concentrate, "nearest" loses
meaning, and irrelevant features actively hurt. Select features or reduce
dimension first.

Also sensitive to: class imbalance (the majority class wins votes by
sheer count — use distance weighting or resampling), and to memory, since the
entire training set must be kept and shipped.

Where it shines: small-to-medium low-dimensional data, recommender
systems, anomaly detection via k-distance, imputation
(KNNImputer), and as an honest baseline for anything.
Interview corner
Q. Why is KNN called a lazy learner?

Because fit() does no generalisation — it only stores the data. All
computation is deferred to prediction. The consequence is $O(1)$ training and
$O(nd)$ per query, the reverse of every eager learner.
Q. How do you choose k?

Cross-validation over a range of odd values. Never training error — it is
minimised at $k=1$ by construction, since each point is its own nearest
neighbour. A rough starting point is $k\approx\sqrt{n}$, then tune around it.
Q. Why must features be scaled?

Distance is a sum over features, so a feature with a large numeric range
dominates it and the others are ignored. Unlike a linear model, KNN has no
weights that can rescale a feature's influence.
Q. What is the curse of dimensionality for KNN?

As $d$ grows, all pairwise distances converge to the same value, so the nearest
neighbours are not meaningfully nearer than random points. Data density also
falls exponentially, so a "local" neighbourhood covers most of each feature's
range. KNN needs low dimension or aggressive feature selection.
Q. Euclidean or Manhattan?

Euclidean by default. Manhattan is more robust when individual features have
outliers and often works better in higher dimensions, since it concentrates
less. Treat $p$ as a hyperparameter and tune it.
Q. How does KNN handle imbalanced classes?

Badly, by default — the majority class wins on raw counts even when the
minority is closer. Use weights="distance", resample, or use
RadiusNeighborsClassifier so density rather than count decides.
Q. KNN vs K-Means — what is the relationship?

None, beyond the letter K. KNN is supervised classification/regression with $k$
= number of neighbours consulted. K-Means is unsupervised clustering with $k$ =
number of clusters. They share no objective, no training procedure, and no
output type.
Q. Can KNN give probabilities?

Yes — the fraction of the $k$ neighbours in each class (weighted, if
weights="distance"). They are coarse, taking only $k+1$ distinct values
with uniform weights, and are poorly calibrated for small $k$.
Q. How would you deploy KNN with 50 million rows?

Not exactly. Use an approximate nearest-neighbour index (FAISS, HNSW, ScaNN)
which trades a little recall for sub-linear queries, reduce dimension first
with PCA or a learned embedding, and consider replacing KNN with a model whose
prediction cost does not grow with the training set.
Worked Examples
Classifying one point with $k=3$
Training points: class A $=\{(1,1),(2,1),(2,2)\}$; class B $=\{(6,5),(7,6),(6,6)\}$. Query point $q = (3,2)$, Euclidean distance.
Step 1 – distances.
Step 2 – vote. The three nearest are all class A, so the prediction is A (with $k=5$, the vote is 3 A to 2 B, still A).
Step 3 – what changes with scale. If the second feature were in units 1000 times larger, distances would be dominated by it and the neighbours would change. Always scale before KNN.
Cost. Prediction computes all 6 distances here; with $N$ training rows it is $O(N)$ per query, which is why KNN is slow at inference on large data.
